vignette:
Mira is thirty-five years old and has been a physical therapist at a suburban rehabilitation clinic for six years. She is married to David, a gentle, soft-spoken accountant, and they live in a small house with a garden. Her patients trust her—she is patient, precise, and kind. But what they do not see is the clock ticking inside her chest, counting the minutes until she can retreat to a room with no windows.

The story of what haunts her began seven years ago, before David, before the clinic. She was living with a man named Evan, a marketing executive whose praise felt like sunlight and whose rage felt like a door slamming shut. The first time he struck her, he apologized with tears in his eyes. She believed him. Over the next eighteen months, the apologies grew shorter, the bruises deeper, and the intervals of calm shrank until she could no longer recognize the shape of a safe day.

She remembers the weight of his hand on her throat, the way he would whisper “you made me do this” into her hair. She remembers the smell of his cologne and the sound of the front door lock clicking after he left for work. She remembers looking at her own reflection and seeing a stranger’s hollow eyes.

She left after a broken rib—hollowed out, quiet, and afraid of her own shadow. She met David a year later. He is kind. He has never raised his voice. She married him because she thought love could erase memory. It cannot.

Now, at the clinic, she works with a patient who reminds her of Evan—the same broad shoulders, the same way of laughing. Mira’s hands shake when she guides him through hamstring stretches. She shortens the session, invents a scheduling conflict. She avoids him on the treatment floor. At night, she lies rigid beside David, listening for footsteps that are not there. She has not slept through the night in four years.

Her PCL-5 score of 79 reflects what she feels every day: intrusive images of Evan’s face contorted with anger, a cold sweat when a door closes too loudly, a compulsion to check the locks even when David is home. She startles when David touches her from behind. She has stopped going to the grocery store alone because the aisles feel like corridors. She avoids the left side of the bed, the side where Evan used to sleep.

Her work is a double-edged sword. Physical contact is her profession, but every hand she holds, every shoulder she palpates, demands that she override a survival instinct screaming *danger*. She has become deft at dissociation: she can count repetitions, measure range of motion, and speak in a calm voice while her mind is somewhere else—watching herself from the ceiling, nodding, performing the role of a therapist.

She has never told David about Evan’s hands on her neck. She tells herself it would hurt him to know, but the truth is that saying it aloud would make it real again. So she carries the story inside her like a locked box.

Today, after her last patient, Mira sits in her car in the parking lot. She stares at the dashboard. The sun is setting, and she feels an old familiar pressure in her chest—the sense that something terrible is about to happen, that she must be ready. She grips the steering wheel until her knuckles turn white. She waits. The thing does not come. It never comes. But she is always waiting.
